newsitem.title: USA: Alaska atomic site leaks radiation - Greenpeace.
newsitem.headline: Alaska atomic site leaks radiation - Greenpeace.

text.p: Contrary to government findings, the site of the biggest U.S. underground nuclear test on an island off Alaska is leaking radioactivity into the Bering Sea, Greenpeace said on Wednesday.
Amchitka Island in the Aleutian Islands was the site of three underground nuclear tests in the late 1960s and early 1970s, including the single largest underground test called Project Cannikin.
Greenpeace in a report issued 25 years after the blast said the Cannikin site is leaking radiation because the underground explosion occurred too close to the surface.
"Leakage from the Cannikin site is probably extensive, involving groundwater pathways through fissures and through the bottom of Cannikin Lake," the Greenpeace report said.
The study also showed contamination of plant life, meaning the radioactivity entered the food chain, Pam Miller, the study's author, said.

But checks by the Atomic Energy Commission, later replaced by the Energy Department and by the Environmental Protection Agency, have shown only "insignificant" amounts of radioactive vapours, without serious contamination.

After meeting with Greenpeace representatives, Energy Department officials said they will work with them to verify the findings, and will look into how the EPA, which does the government's monitoring, conducts its checks.

Energy Undersecretary Thomas Grumbly said in a telephone briefing that based on Greenpeace's findings, the worst case exposure from the site would be far less than average annual background radiation exposure in the United States.
The island is uninhabited, with some commercial fishing done off its shores, department officials said.
Grumbly also said the department will review the status of documents that Greenpeace complained had been kept secret.
In its report, Greenpeace accused the government of conducting flawed tests and trying to hide mistakes.

The Cannikin blast of five megatons -- equivalent to 5 million tons of dynamite -- was the last of three underground tests at the remote island that is 765 miles (1,231 km) west of the tip of Alaska and 870 miles (1,400 km) east of the Russian Far East.

An expedition Greenpeace sent to the island in June found that the Cannikin site was leaking radioactivity into the Bering Sea through White Alice Creek, which it said disappeared into the crater formed by the blast.
Greenpeace said Americium-241 found in aquatic vegetation showed that Cannikin was leaking long-lived radioactivity through groundwater into surface waters about 1 mile (1.6 km) from ground zero.
